Rial hits record low despite direct bank dollar sales

What happened

Five banks began selling dollars Saturday under the Central Bank’s expanded retail-FX program, allowing adults to buy up to $10,000 with a national ID. Tasnim reported an initial rate of 259,000 tomans per dollar. The Central Bank has outlined an intervention ceiling of $2 billion.

Yet the rial weakened. Reuters cited Bonbast at 268,800 tomans per dollar, versus 263,200 Friday. Donya-e Eqtesad quoted 270,580 alongside a commercial/remittance rate of 175,228, implying a free-market premium of 54.4%.

Background

Unlike preferential or commercial FX allocations, the program gives individuals broader access to cash dollars at near-market prices.

At the $10,000 purchase ceiling, $2 billion would cover 200,000 maximum-size transactions. That says nothing about actual demand, average purchases or the pace of supply. The volume actually sold remains unconfirmed.

Economic significance

The program expands formal dollar supply but may also induce additional demand. Its impact depends on actual sales, pricing and access.

The bank rate was roughly 4% below the free-market rate, creating less arbitrage incentive than heavily subsidized dollar allocations. Continued depreciation suggests the initial intervention did not overcome underlying demand, but without sales data, it is too early to judge effectiveness.

More fundamentally, selling existing reserves does not create new export earnings. A stronger FX balance requires increased usable export receipts, released foreign assets, reduced import demand, improved settlement channels or restored maritime export capacity.

Outlook

The test now shifts from announced commitments to execution.

Several days of sustained dollar availability and a narrowing free-market premium would matter more than a brief appreciation. Continued depreciation despite substantial documented sales would suggest that demand exceeds intervention or that buyers doubt the durability of future supply.

What to watch

Track actual dollars sold, successful purchasers, average transaction size, effective bank rates and uninterrupted availability.

Watch the commercial/remittance rate separately. Stabilizing cash-dollar trading does not necessarily lower the FX cost of imports or industrial inputs.

Hundreds of thousands filled Seoul's streets today, some accusing China of helping install their own president.

On October 3, South Korea's National Foundation Day, multiple rallies converged downtown. The largest, organized by civic groups on Sejong-daero, drew a police estimate of 140,000, with organizer claims reaching as high as 500,000. Separately, the main opposition party held its own rally near Namdaemun with over 60 sitting lawmakers.

The anger spans several fronts. Protesters demanded President Lee Jae-myung's impeachment and a return to his suspended criminal trials. They pointed to a September 21 land-mine blast at the DMZ that injured three soldiers, which Lee called an "unfortunate accident." They criticized a new prosecution reform that stripped investigative powers from prosecutors, plans to expand the Supreme Court, and rising home prices alongside falling stocks.

Some protesters went further, using anti-CCP language and alleging the 2025 election that brought Lee to power was rigged with Chinese involvement. That claim remains unproven and wasn't part of the mainstream opposition party's message, which focused on security and the economy instead.
